vignette:
Martin is a 54-year-old civil servant of British descent who presented for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of distress he had, until recently, struggled to name. He lives with his current partner of two years and works in a regional government office, and on the surface his life carries the appearance of quiet stability. Beneath it, however, he has been managing the aftermath of a relationship that ended three years ago - one in which he was repeatedly physically assaulted by the woman he had loved and, for a long time, continued to protect.

The abuse unfolded over the course of a four-year relationship. His former partner's violence was unpredictable and often nocturnal: she would strike him at night, sometimes while he was half-asleep, and the attacks frequently occurred when no one else was present in the house. On one occasion that Martin returns to with particular frequency, he had been alone with her in the kitchen after dinner. He had said something she interpreted as a slight, and before he could process what was happening she had him pinned against the counter, her hands at his throat, his own hands held down. He remembered the metallic tang of blood from where he had bitten the inside of his cheek, and the particular quality of helplessness - not just physical but cognitive, the sense that his own judgment about what was safe had completely failed him.

In the months after the relationship ended, Martin noticed that certain moments seemed to arrive without warning and with a strange, arrested quality - less like recollections than like stilled images, vivid and flat at once, as though he were flipping through photographs of something that had happened to someone else. The taste of blood could return without any apparent prompt, and in those moments the distance he normally maintained from the past collapsed entirely. When he tried to sit down and deliberately recall what had happened - to make sense of it, to construct a coherent account - he found the memory strangely inaccessible, slipping away from any direct attempt to hold it. This inconsistency bewildered him and had come to feel, in itself, like evidence of something broken in him.

What Martin had come to believe, with a quiet but firm certainty, was that he was fundamentally unsafe when alone - particularly alone with men. At work, this had consequences. His office required him at times to attend small internal meetings, and when those meetings left him one-on-one with a male colleague in a closed room, he would find reasons to leave early, prop the door open, or reschedule. Over eighteen months this had earned him a reputation for being difficult to pin down, and a performance review had noted his reluctance to engage in direct bilateral communication. He had not told anyone why. Being alone in any room or building had gradually become something he organised his entire day around avoiding, and he had developed a habit of arriving at work early specifically to ensure he was never the last to leave. Evenings at home when his partner worked late had become ordeals he managed by calling friends, attending whatever was available - a pub quiz, a neighbour's dinner - anything to keep himself surrounded by other voices until she returned. Sleeping alone, when she travelled, was something he had stopped doing entirely; on those nights he stayed with his brother.

The detachment he applied to the memories was effortful and deliberate - a kind of internal turning away that he had practised until it became reflex - and the constant company he kept served a similar purpose: as long as there were people around him, there was no silence in which the photographs could appear.

What finally brought Martin to seek help was a conversation with his current partner, who had gently observed that she did not know him - that he seemed always to be managing something she was not permitted to see. He had found he could not reassure her, because he knew she was right. What he feared most, coming into therapy, was that examining what had happened would confirm what he already half-believed: that the man who had been unable to stop it was the man he still was. What he hoped for, more quietly, was that this might not be true.
